lessons.title: Addition Fluency Within 10
lessons.explanation: Develop reliable addition fluency for sums within TEN. Explain a helpful known fact, count on, or ten-frame strategy rather than guessing.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 6+4=10, two parts make a ten. Example 2: 5+3=8 by starting at five and counting three more. Example 3: 4+4=8 is a known double.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Read the addends (sum no more than 10). Step 2: Try a familiar fact, double or count-on. Step 3: State the sum accurately. Step 4: Check with counters or related fact.
lessons.mistakes: Do not confuse speed with accuracy or use a sum above ten as evidence of fluency within ten.
lessons.summary: I can find sums within ten using facts and a strategy I understand.

lessons.title: Relate Addition and Subtraction
lessons.explanation: Relate addition and subtraction within ten as inverse number relationships. A single set of three numbers can yield a fact family.
lessons.examples: Example 1: If 5+4=9, then 9-4=5 and 9-5=4. Example 2: 6+3=9 and 9-6=3.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Find two parts and their whole, at most ten. Step 2: Write a true addition fact. Step 3: Begin a subtraction with the whole. Step 4: Remove one part to find the other. Step 5: Check.
lessons.mistakes: Do not write 5-9=4 for a within-ten part-whole fact; start subtraction from the whole nine.
lessons.summary: I can use addition to explain and check subtraction.

lessons.title: Add and Subtract Within 20 PLC Activity
lessons.explanation: PLC: add and subtract within TWENTY, using different helpful strategies and explaining why they work. Partner discussion remains teacher-led.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Decide whether to add or subtract. Step 2: Choose making ten, known fact or count-on. Step 3: Show an equivalent calculation. Step 4: Check with inverse operation. Step 5: Explain the choice.
lessons.mistakes: Do not lose leftover ones when making ten or treat a teacher conversation as complete merely by submitting a numeric answer.
lessons.summary: I can use efficient addition and subtraction strategies within twenty.

lessons.title: Change Unknown Story Problems PLC Activity
lessons.explanation: Solve Add To or Take From stories where the CHANGE is unknown. Identify the known start and final amount, and find what joined or left.
lessons.examples: Example 1: Seven birds, then some join, now twelve: 7+□=12; five joined. Example 2: Fifteen counters, some removed, now nine: 15-□=9; six removed.
lessons.steps: Step 1: State the starting count and result count. Step 2: Determine whether the story adds or removes. Step 3: Put the box in the CHANGE position. Step 4: Solve and check against the story.
lessons.mistakes: Do not automatically place the box at the result: in 7+□=12 the missing number is 5.
lessons.summary: I can find the unknown change in joining or leaving stories.

lessons.title: Put Together and Take Apart Story Problems
lessons.explanation: Solve Put Together/Take Apart stories with an unknown ADDEND or missing part. Use a part-whole model or addition/subtraction relation.
lessons.examples: Example 1: There are 13 marbles; eight are blue and the rest are red. 8+□=13, so five are red. Example 2: Two groups together have 17, one group has nine: 9+□=17, missing part eight.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify the whole. Step 2: Name the given part and unknown part. Step 3: Write part+part=whole. Step 4: Solve the missing addend. Step 5: Check that parts sum to the whole.
lessons.mistakes: Do not add the whole to the known part; the whole already contains both parts.
lessons.summary: I can solve a missing-part Put Together/Take Apart story.

lessons.title: Compare Story Problems
lessons.explanation: Solve Compare stories with DIFFERENCE UNKNOWN. Identify the larger and smaller quantities and explain the difference without confusing it with their total.
lessons.examples: Example 1: Sara has 12 stickers and Kim has 7. Sara has five more because 12-7=5. Example 2: A 16-cube tower and a 9-cube tower differ by seven cubes.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Identify what quantities are compared and their units. Step 2: Mark which is larger. Step 3: Subtract smaller from larger or count on. Step 4: State how many more or fewer. Step 5: Check by adding difference to smaller.
lessons.mistakes: Do not answer 19 stickers for 'how many more' when comparing 12 and 7; 19 is a total, not a difference.
lessons.summary: I can solve a Compare story to find the difference.

lessons.title: Count Large Collections
lessons.explanation: Count, organize and represent up to 120 objects starting the count from an arbitrary number, not necessarily one. Use tens groups to track large collections.
lessons.examples: Example 1: Count on from 87: 88,89,90,91. Example 2: Eleven tens and six ones make 116. Example 3: Count from 109 to 110,111,112.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Read the starting number. Step 2: Count on by ones, regrouping at a new ten or hundred. Step 3: Make full tens groups when counting a collection. Step 4: Record and check the total, at most 120.
lessons.mistakes: Do not restart from one when a different start is specified, or skip 110 after 109.
lessons.summary: I can count and represent large collections and start from a number other than one.

lessons.title: Show Me All the Ways PLC Activity
lessons.explanation: PLC: REPRESENT a two-digit number in different valid ways using tens, ones, base-ten drawings and expanded addition. Replacing one ten with ten ones does not change the total.
lessons.examples: Example 1: 54=5 tens 4 ones=4 tens 14 ones. Example 2: 68=60+8=5 tens 18 ones. Example 3: 73=70+3.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Write or build the original two-digit number. Step 2: Show tens-and-ones model. Step 3: Break one ten into ten ones for an alternative. Step 4: Compare totals to verify equivalent representations.
lessons.mistakes: Do not read 4 tens 14 ones as 414; it is 40+14=54. Classroom comparison requires a real partner or teacher.
lessons.summary: I can create and compare different representations of the same number.

lessons.title: Solve Number Riddles
lessons.explanation: Solve mathematical NUMBER RIDDLES using place value clues, unknown quantities and true equations. Check each proposed clue, not just one.
lessons.examples: Example 1: I have six tens and five ones: the number is 65. Example 2: I am 10 less than 75: the number is 65. Both clues match. Example 3: If a clue says 60=25+45, reject it because 25+45=70.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Read every clue. Step 2: Turn each clue into a number relation. Step 3: Propose a possible number. Step 4: Check all clues and reject contradictions. Step 5: Explain your answer.
lessons.mistakes: Do not accept a false equality just because it resembles the correct number. 60 is not equal to 25+45.
lessons.summary: I can solve number riddles and prove a candidate satisfies all clues.

lessons.title: Write Number Riddles
lessons.explanation: Create an ORIGINAL number riddle using place-value clues and a truthful addition/subtraction relation, then solve it and check uniqueness when requested. Authorship and clarity need teacher assessment.
lessons.examples: Example 1: I am between 40 and 50, have 4 tens and 7 ones, and am 10 more than 37. I am 47. Example 2: I have six tens and two ones, and am 10 less than 72: I am 62.
lessons.steps: Step 1: Choose a target two-digit number. Step 2: Write independent true clues about tens, ones, or ten more/less. Step 3: Check every equation and clue. Step 4: Ask another person to solve it. Step 5: Revise if clues are wrong or unclear.
lessons.mistakes: Do not invent a clue inconsistent with your own target: if the number is 47, 'ten more than 47' is 57, not 47. A generated prompt cannot prove student originality.
lessons.summary: I can write an accurate number riddle and explain its solution.
